ideas.title: Electricity took forty years to pay off
ideas.idea:
A new technology rarely pays off until people redesign the work around it, and that can take a generation.

By 1900 electric power had been on sale for two decades, yet American factories were barely more productive. Owners had swapped a big steam engine for a big electric motor and kept everything else: the overhead line shaft, the belts, the machines lined up wherever the shaft ran. Electricity's real gift was that every machine could have its own small motor, so a factory could be laid out around the flow of work instead of the route of the power. Lighter, single-storey, safer plants followed, but only as old mills wore out and managers learned to think differently. Productivity finally leapt in the 1920s.

The economist Paul David told this story in 1990 to explain why computers weren't yet showing up in the statistics.
why: Paul David (Stanford), 'The Dynamo and the Computer', American Economic Review, 1990: electric motors drove under 5% of US factory machinery in 1899 and just over half by the early 1920s; their spread accounts for about half the 1920s jump in manufacturing productivity growth.
Tim Harford (Financial Times) adds a human side: the gains also needed retrained workers with more responsibility, nudged by WWI-era limits on cheap labour.
Caveat: David himself warns the analogy is loose. Computers differ from dynamos, and a past lag doesn't predict a timetable for any technology today.

ideas.deep_dive:
Paul David, an economic historian at Stanford, set out the argument in a 1990 paper called "The Dynamo and the Computer". Edison's Pearl Street station began selling electricity in Manhattan in 1882, yet in 1899 electric motors still supplied under 5% of the mechanical drive in American factories. By the early 1920s it was just over half.

The delay wasn't stubbornness. A steam-powered factory was built around one huge engine turning a long overhead shaft, with leather belts dropping down to each machine. Buildings were tall and narrow to keep the shafts short, and machines sat wherever the power was, not where the work needed them. Swapping the steam engine for one big electric motor changed very little.

The real gain came with "unit drive": a small motor on every machine. Now a factory could be a single storey, laid out in the order the work flowed, with better light and no forest of belts. But that meant new buildings, new layouts and new habits, so it happened as old mills wore out and a new generation of managers took charge.

Economists now see this as the normal pattern for a general-purpose technology. Before it pays, firms must make a pile of invisible investments: retraining, reorganising, inventing new processes. Erik Brynjolfsson and colleagues call the resulting dip-then-rise in measured productivity the "productivity J-curve". It describes a tendency, not a timetable.

examples.title: Ford rearranges the work, 1913–14
examples.text: At Ford's Highland Park plant in Detroit, machine tools were laid out in the sequence the work needed, not grouped by type. In April 1913 the flywheel magneto moved onto a moving line, and the labour time per unit fell from about 20 minutes to five. By early 1914, three continuous lines were finishing a Model T every 93 minutes, against 12½ hours under the old stationary method. The gain came from reorganising the work, not from a new machine.

examples.title: Computers in the 1980s
examples.text: In 1987 the economist Robert Solow quipped that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. David's dynamo paper was partly a reply: give it time. US productivity growth did pick up from the mid-1990s, once firms reorganised retail, logistics and offices around networked computers rather than simply putting a PC on every desk.

examples.title: AI today
examples.text: Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson argue AI is following the same path. Firms must first invest heavily in data, new workflows and skills, and that spending doesn't show up as extra output straight away. So measured productivity can sag before it rises. How long AI's J-curve lasts is an open question.

ideas.title: Praise didn't make them worse
ideas.idea:
When something unusually good or bad happens, the next result will probably be closer to average, whatever you do. Daniel Kahneman learned this working with Israeli Air Force flight instructors. One insisted that praise backfired: cadets he praised for a superb manoeuvre usually flew worse next time, while those he shouted at improved. The pattern was real, but the cause was luck. An exceptional flight is partly skill and partly a good day, and good days don't repeat on demand, so the next attempt drifts back towards the cadet's normal level, praise or no praise.

The same trap catches the manager who 'fixes' a terrible quarter, the remedy taken at the worst point of a cold, and the club that sacks its coach after a losing run. Before crediting or blaming an intervention, ask whether things would have drifted back anyway.
why: Kahneman tells the story in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), chapter 17.
Statisticians call it regression to the mean: wherever results mix skill with chance, extreme scores tend to be followed by less extreme ones. Francis Galton first described it in the 1880s.
Caveat: this doesn't mean feedback is useless. It means you need a comparison group, or many attempts, to tell whether it worked.

ideas.deep_dive:
Any result that mixes skill with luck can be split in two: your underlying level, plus a random part that changes every time. When a result is extreme, the random part was probably extreme too, and it won't repeat on demand. So the next result tends to land nearer the middle. Nothing has to cause the change; it's built into the arithmetic.

Francis Galton spotted it in the 1880s while comparing the heights of parents and their grown children. Very tall parents had tall children, but on average less tall than themselves; very short parents had children who were short, but less so. He called it "regression towards mediocrity". Statisticians now call it regression to the mean.

The trap is psychological. We notice extremes, act on them, then watch things return to normal and credit our action. The flight instructor praised after unusually good flights and shouted after unusually bad ones, so praise was always followed by a dip and shouting by a rise. Kahneman drew a bleak conclusion: because of regression, people who reward good work and punish bad work will tend to see punishment appear to work better.

The fix is a fair comparison: a similar group that didn't get the treatment, or the long-run average rather than the last result. The effect is strongest where luck plays a big part, and weakest where performance is mostly skill.

examples.title: Israeli flight school, 1960s
examples.text: Kahneman was teaching Israeli Air Force instructors that praise works better than punishment when one objected: cadets he praised after a great manoeuvre usually did worse next time, and those he screamed at improved. Kahneman realised both were just returning to their normal level. He had the instructors throw coins at a target behind their backs to show that the best and worst throws were rarely repeated, with no feedback at all.

examples.title: Speed cameras in Britain
examples.text: Cameras usually go where there has just been a cluster of crashes, which is exactly when numbers are likely to fall anyway. A simple before-and-after count flatters them. When Professor Richard Allsop of UCL studied 551 fixed cameras across nine areas for the RAC Foundation in 2013, he corrected for regression to the mean. Even then, fatal and serious collisions near the cameras fell by 27% on average: real, but smaller than raw figures suggested.

examples.title: The 'cover jinx'
examples.text: Athletes tend to land on the cover of Sports Illustrated after an exceptional run, and often slump soon after, which fed a long-running superstition that the cover is cursed. The likelier explanation, as Ben Goldacre notes in Bad Science, is that an exceptional run is partly luck, and the next stretch drifts back towards the athlete's usual level.

ideas.title: The 'wood wide web' is mostly hype
ideas.idea: Trees probably aren't chatting through underground fungal networks, at least not the way bestsellers suggest. Mycorrhizal fungi are real and vital: they wrap tree roots, trading water and nutrients for sugar, and some link several trees at once. But in 2023 three forest ecologists led by Justine Karst at the University of Alberta reviewed the field evidence for three popular claims: that these networks are widespread in forests, that big trees feed seedlings through them, and that trees use them to send warnings. Each claim turned out to be thinly supported. Only two studies had actually mapped shared fungal links between trees, and seedlings connected to networks did no better on average. Meanwhile, citations overstating the original results had nearly doubled over 25 years. A good story had outrun its data.
why: Karst, Jones and Hoeksema, Nature Ecology & Evolution (2023), reviewed 26 seedling studies and more than 1,600 papers citing 18 key field studies.
The authors call the drift 'positive citation bias': each retelling slightly overstated what the original study showed.
Caveat: the fungi themselves are essential to forest health. The doubt is about network-wide sharing and signalling, not about mycorrhizae.

visual.label: Justine Karst on the 'wood wide web' — Sentientism

ideas.deep_dive:
Mycorrhizal fungi are not in doubt. Most trees depend on them: fungal threads wrap around or enter the roots and reach far into the soil, swapping water and nutrients for sugars from the tree. Some of the same fungi can attach to more than one tree, forming what scientists call common mycorrhizal networks.

The excitement began with a 1997 paper in Nature by Suzanne Simard and colleagues in British Columbia, which made the journal's cover. They reported carbon moving between paper birch and Douglas fir in the field, with more reaching firs that were shaded. Over the following decades the finding grew in the retelling into "mother trees" nursing their offspring and forests warning each other of attack through a "wood wide web".

In 2023 Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema checked the field evidence behind three popular claims. Are networks widespread in forests? Only two studies had actually mapped shared fungal links between trees. Do seedlings benefit from joining one? Across 26 studies, neutral effects were the most common result. Do trees send warnings through them? The only test was a greenhouse experiment on potted seedlings. They also traced more than 1,600 papers citing 18 key field studies, and found the rate of citations claiming more than the study showed had almost doubled in 25 years.

The limit cuts both ways. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence: networks may matter in some forests. The point is that the confident popular story ran well ahead of the data.

examples.title: A Nature cover, 1997
examples.text: Simard's team tracked carbon between paper birch and Douglas fir seedlings growing in a British Columbia forest, and found a net flow towards the firs, larger when the firs were shaded. Nature put the study on its cover, and the network soon became known as the "wood wide web". It was a careful experiment. The trouble came later, as the result was repeated more grandly than it had been measured.

examples.title: From journal to bestseller
examples.text: Peter Wohlleben's The Hidden Life of Trees (2015) became an international bestseller with its picture of trees sharing food and caring for their young, and the idea spread through podcasts, TV and documentaries. Karst's team argue that each retelling, in public and in parts of the scientific literature, drifted further from what the field studies actually showed.

examples.title: Forestry on trial
examples.text: The Mother Tree Project, launched by Simard in 2015, runs long-term research sites across British Columbia. It tests how many large trees to leave standing during logging, and which seedlings to replant, and measures the effects on regrowth, biodiversity and carbon. That's the right kind of test. Karst's warning is that forest rules shouldn't assume network benefits before such results are in.

ideas.title: We overvalue what we build
ideas.idea:
Putting your own effort into making something makes you value it more, even when the result is mediocre. Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely called this the IKEA effect. Across four studies, people assembled IKEA storage boxes, folded origami and built Lego sets, then put a value on their work. They rated their amateur creations as similar in value to versions made by experts, and expected other people to agree. The extra love only appeared when the job was finished: when people built something and then had to take it apart, or never completed it, the effect faded.

It explains a lot at work: why teams defend their own designs, why 'not invented here' thinking is so stubborn, and why whoever built the spreadsheet struggles to see its flaws.
why: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 'The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love', Journal of Consumer Psychology (2012).
The effect held for keen DIYers and complete novices alike, and depended on successfully completing the task.
Caveat: the items were cheap and simple, and the extra value lives mainly in the builder's eyes. A buyer won't share it.
Ariely has faced data-integrity questions over other studies. This effect has been independently replicated (Sarstedt and colleagues, 2017).

visual.label: Dan Ariely: What makes us feel good about our work? — TED
visual.note: Starts at 12:36 with IKEA and the cake-mix story (now disputed), then the origami experiment.

ideas.deep_dive:
Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely published the first tests in 2011. In one, students either assembled a plain IKEA storage box or were handed one already built, then said what they'd pay for it. The builders bid 63% more. In another, people folded origami cranes and frogs from instructions. Builders valued their own lumpy models about five times as highly as onlookers did, and roughly as highly as onlookers valued models folded by experts.

Two details matter. First, the effect needed success: when people built something and then had to take it apart, or didn't finish, the extra love largely faded. Second, it lived in the builder's head. Other people didn't share the valuation, which is why the effect can mislead makers about what their work is worth to anyone else.

Why does it happen? The authors link it to effort justification (we like what cost us something) and to feeling competent: finishing a task is proof we're capable, and the object becomes a trophy of that. Follow-up work by Mochon and colleagues tied the effect to restoring a dented sense of competence.

It's a mixed blessing. A little effort can deepen commitment, which is why some products deliberately leave the customer part of the job. But it also explains why we cling to our own plans, code and spreadsheets long after an outsider would have scrapped them.

examples.title: Loom bands, 2017
examples.text: A team led by Marko Sarstedt repeated the idea with a different craft: making loom-band bracelets. Builders again put a higher value on their own creations, and when the creations were destroyed, their willingness to pay dropped significantly. That matches the original finding that the extra value depends on having a finished result, and shows the effect isn't specific to flat-pack furniture.

examples.title: Meal kits
examples.text: Food brands lean on the effect with "ready to create" meal kits and curry kits that leave the customer some of the cooking. Nielsen estimated more than a million Australian households would be buying meal kits by the end of 2019. The pitch isn't only convenience; it's the satisfaction of having made dinner yourself, with the hard parts done.

examples.title: The cake-mix legend
examples.text: The most famous example is probably a myth. The story goes that 1950s instant cake mixes sold poorly until makers told cooks to add a fresh egg, giving them a sense of having baked. Food historian Laura Shapiro found fresh eggs mainly helped because dried egg made worse cakes, and fresh-egg patents date back to the 1930s. The effect is real; the favourite anecdote isn't.

ideas.title: Most of your fears never arrive
ideas.idea:
Much of what we dread hurts more in anticipation than it ever does in reality. Seneca made the point to his friend Lucilius nearly 2,000 years ago, writing that we "suffer more often in imagination than in reality". He offered a simple audit for any looming worry. Is it certain, or just rumour and suspicion? Is it truly harmful, or merely embarrassing? Is it happening now, or might it never come? Time, he noted, often intervenes: threats fade, get postponed or turn into something else. Meanwhile, the worrier has already paid in full.

This isn't advice to ignore risks. It's a way to separate a real problem you can act on today from a story your mind is running ahead of the facts.
why: Seneca, Letter 13 of the Moral Letters to Lucilius (around AD 65), quoted in Richard Gummere's 1917 translation.
Modern cognitive behavioural therapy uses a similar move, asking people to test anxious predictions against the evidence.
Caveat: some fears are accurate. The aim is to weigh them honestly, not to dismiss them.

ideas.deep_dive:
Seneca, adviser to the emperor Nero and one of the leading Stoic writers, wrote 124 letters of practical philosophy to his friend Lucilius late in life. Letter 13 is about groundless fear. His point isn't that bad things never happen. It's that we suffer them early, often and in exaggerated form, through anticipation.

His method is an audit. First, separate what you know from what you've heard or assumed: many fears rest on rumour. Second, ask whether the thing is truly harmful or merely unpleasant or embarrassing. Third, ask whether it is happening now or only might. Even likely troubles are uncertain in timing and form, and many expected blows never land, or arrive in a different shape. He also suggests weighing hope against fear: when the outcome is genuinely uncertain, there's no reason to rehearse only the worst version.

The Stoics paired this with a deliberate practice, premeditatio malorum, rehearsing misfortunes in advance. It sounds like the opposite, but the aim is the same: look at the feared thing calmly and in detail, so it loses its vague power, and plan what you would actually do.

Modern cognitive behavioural therapy does something similar when it asks anxious people to write predictions down and check them against what happened. The limit: some fears are accurate, and some people's circumstances really are dangerous. The audit is for sorting fears, not dismissing them.

examples.title: A worry log at Penn State
examples.text: Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman asked 29 people with generalised anxiety disorder to write down their worries for ten days, then check about 20 days later which had come true. 91.4% of the worry predictions did not. The most common result was that none of a person's worries came true. Those who saw most clearly how often their worries were wrong also improved most in treatment. It's a small study, but it puts numbers on Seneca's hunch.

examples.title: Fear-setting
examples.text: Tim Ferriss turned Seneca's idea into a written exercise he calls fear-setting, set out in a 2017 TED talk. Write down the move you're dreading. List the worst outcomes and, for each, how you could prevent it and how you'd repair the damage. Then list the benefits of trying, and the cost of doing nothing in six months, a year and three years. He credits the exercise with much of his success.

images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

ideas.title: Working complex systems start simple
ideas.idea:
If you want a complex system that works, start with a simple one that works and grow it. That's Gall's Law, from the paediatrician John Gall's 1975 book General Systemantics, a tongue-in-cheek study of why systems fail. His observation: every complex system that works turns out to have evolved from a simpler system that worked, while a complex system designed from scratch never works and can't be patched into working. You have to go back and start again with something simple.

Engineers recognise it in the internet, which grew from a four-computer network in 1969, and in the advice to build a minimum viable product first. It also explains why big-bang IT rollouts so often go wrong: too many untested interactions at once, and no working baseline to fall back to.
why: John Gall, General Systemantics (1975), later republished as Systemantics and The Systems Bible.
The same logic underpins iterative engineering: prototype, test, then add complexity one verified step at a time.
Caveat: it's a rule of thumb from experience, not a proven law. Some well-specified systems are designed whole and work, though usually from proven parts.

visual.label: A brief history of the World Wide Web — CERN
visual.note: See how small the Web was at the start: one computer, one site, a few simple rules.

ideas.deep_dive:
John Gall was an American paediatrician, not an engineer, and General Systemantics is written as satire. But its central rule has been quoted by software architects for decades, because it matches experience: a working complex system is the end of a long series of working simpler ones.

The reason is interactions. In a simple system you can see every part and test how they fit. Each addition can be checked against a version that already works, so when something breaks you know where to look. A complex system designed in one go has thousands of interactions nobody has ever seen together. When it fails, it fails everywhere at once, and there's no working version to fall back on. Patching rarely helps, because each fix adds new interactions.

Growing a system also lets reality do some of the design. Real users, data and load reveal what's actually needed, which no specification fully anticipates. That's why agile software, minimum viable products and staged rollouts all start small on purpose.

The limits: Gall's Law is a rule of thumb, not physics. Some systems must be big from day one, and well-understood engineering, like a bridge, can be designed whole because its parts and interactions are already proven. Even then, the safest big launches are assembled from components that have each worked before.

examples.title: The Web beat Xanadu
examples.text: Ted Nelson began Project Xanadu in 1960, aiming for a perfect hypertext system with two-way links, version tracking and built-in royalties. An incomplete version appeared only in 1998, and a working release in 2014. Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal at CERN was far cruder: one-way links that could break, simple pages and a basic protocol, running on a single NeXT computer. Simple enough to work at once, it grew into the Web.

image.caption: The NeXT computer at CERN that Tim Berners-Lee used as the first web server.
image.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

examples.title: The NHS National Programme for IT
examples.text: England's plan to give every NHS patient a national electronic record was approved in 2002 as one centrally specified system. By August 2011, £7.3 billion had been spent, MPs urged ministers to scrap it, and it was dismantled that September; estimates of the total cost reached about £10 billion. The government acknowledged the "weaknesses of a top-down, centrally imposed IT system".

examples.title: HealthCare.gov's first day
examples.text: The US federal health-insurance marketplace launched nationwide on 1 October 2013 and buckled under its complexity and traffic. Notes from the launch team, released later, showed that just six people managed to enrol on the first day.

ideas.title: Hanoi's rat bounty bred more rats
ideas.idea:
Pay people per result and they'll find the cheapest way to produce that result, not the outcome you wanted. In 1902, French colonial officials in Hanoi were alarmed by rats swarming from the city's new sewers while plague spread across Asia. They offered a bounty of one cent per rat, and to spare officials from handling carcasses, a tail was enough proof. Soon tailless rats were spotted running through the streets: hunters were cutting off tails and releasing the animals to breed. Health inspectors later found rat farms on the city's outskirts, and the scheme was scrapped.

The historian Michael Vann, who found the story in French archives, points out it's better documented than the famous 'cobra effect'. The lesson: whenever you reward a measurable proxy, ask how someone could game it.
why: Michael G. Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003) and The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt (Oxford University Press, 2018).
Economists call this a perverse incentive, a close cousin of Goodhart's law: a measure stops being useful once it becomes a target.
Caveat: some details, such as how widespread the rat farms were, come from colonial reports and may be exaggerated.

ideas.deep_dive:
In 1897 Paul Doumer arrived as Governor-General of French Indochina and set about turning Hanoi into a showpiece colonial capital, including a modern sewer system for the French quarter. The sewers turned out to be ideal rat habitat. With bubonic plague moving through Asia, the authorities first hired rat catchers, then in 1902 opened the hunt to everyone: one cent per rat, paid on presentation of a tail.

At first it looked like a triumph. In the last week of April, 7,985 rats were killed; by late May, more than 4,000 a day; on 21 June, 20,112 in a single day. But officials began noticing live rats without tails. Hunters had worked out that a tailless rat could keep breeding and supply more tails later. Inspectors then found people farming rats on the city's outskirts. The bounty was dropped, and plague reached Hanoi anyway: an outbreak in 1906 killed at least 263 people.

The mechanism is general. A reward has to be paid on something you can check cheaply: a tail, a target, a number. People then optimise the checkable thing, sometimes at the expense of the real goal. The further the measure is from the outcome, and the bigger the reward, the stronger the pull to game it.

The limits: incentives often work as intended, and gaming isn't inevitable. The lesson is to design them expecting to be tested: check the outcome as well as the proxy, and watch for early signs of cheating.

examples.title: Wells Fargo's sales targets
examples.text: For years Wells Fargo pushed branch staff to sell more products per customer, at one point aiming for eight, under quotas employees described as unrealistic. Staff hit the numbers by opening millions of accounts customers hadn't asked for, including signing people up for online banking who had no internet access. The practice came to light in 2016, and in February 2020 the bank agreed to pay $3 billion to settle criminal and civil investigations.

examples.title: Mexico City's driving ban
examples.text: In 1989 Mexico City banned most cars from the roads one weekday a week, based on the last digit of the number plate. The economist Lucas Davis studied years of hourly pollution data and found no improvement in air quality. Many households simply bought a second car, often an older and dirtier one, so the rule added cars to the road, while bus and metro use didn't rise.

images.caption: A French Indochina one-cent coin of 1902, the bounty paid per rat's tail.
images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

ideas.title: You have about 4,000 weeks
ideas.idea:
If you live to 80, you get just over 4,000 weeks. Oliver Burkeman built his 2021 book Four Thousand Weeks around that uncomfortable number, and his conclusion runs against most productivity advice: you will never get on top of everything, so stop trying. Becoming more efficient doesn't free you; it invites more tasks to fill the space, the way clearing your inbox earns you more email.

His alternative is to accept your limits and choose deliberately what to neglect. Decide which few things truly matter, do those first, and let the rest stay undone without guilt. Finitude isn't a problem for better time management to solve. It's what makes your choices mean something in the first place.
why: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals (2021).
His 'efficiency trap' echoes the Jevons paradox: making something easier often means we end up doing more of it.
Caveat: the advice suits people with some control over their time. For many, the real constraint is workload, not mindset.

ideas.deep_dive:
The number is simple arithmetic: 80 years is about 4,160 weeks. Burkeman's point is what follows from taking it seriously. There will always be more worthwhile things to do than time to do them, so the goal of "getting on top of everything" is impossible by definition. Chasing it makes things worse: get faster at email and you get more email; become known as reliable and you get more requests. He calls this the efficiency trap.

So the real skill isn't doing more; it's choosing what to leave undone, and tolerating the discomfort of that choice. Burkeman suggests habits for it. Keep a strictly limited list of active tasks. Work on one big project at a time and finish it before starting the next. Decide in advance what you'll be mediocre at, so falling short there doesn't sting. Give your most important work the first part of the day, before anything else can claim it.

The idea has old roots. Seneca's essay On the Shortness of Life argued that life is long enough if we don't squander it. Burkeman adds a modern twist: technology promises to give us time back, but mostly fills it.

The limit is real. Much of this assumes some control over your own schedule. For people with caring duties, shift work or two jobs, the constraint is circumstance, not mindset, and no list technique fixes that.

examples.title: A life on one page
examples.text: In 2014 Tim Urban of the Wait But Why blog drew a 90-year human life as a grid of weekly boxes, 52 to a row. It spread widely because it makes the abstract concrete: you can see how many boxes are already filled, and how few, say, summers or visits home remain. It's Burkeman's arithmetic turned into a picture.

examples.title: A ten-item limit
examples.text: Burkeman's own "fixed volume" approach: keep an open list of everything you could do, and a closed list of no more than ten things you're actually working on. Nothing new joins the closed list until something leaves it. The point is to make the trade-off visible, instead of pretending everything will fit if you just work harder.

examples.title: Seneca's version
examples.text: Around two thousand years earlier, Seneca's On the Shortness of Life made a similar case: life feels short mostly because we spend it on things we didn't choose, and keep postponing what matters to a later that may not come.

images.caption: Philippe de Champaigne's Vanitas: tulip, skull and hourglass, a 17th-century reminder that time runs out.

ideas.title: Study the planes that didn't return
ideas.idea:
The evidence in front of you has often been filtered by the very thing you're trying to understand. During the Second World War, the mathematician Abraham Wald, working with Columbia University's Statistical Research Group, studied damage on bombers that came back from missions. The tempting move was to add armour where the bullet holes clustered. Wald's insight was that the sample was missing the planes that never came back. Areas that looked clean on survivors were likely where hits were fatal, so that's where protection mattered most.

The same filter distorts everyday judgement: studying only successful founders, the old buildings still standing, or the customers who stayed. Before drawing a lesson from survivors, ask what the failures would have told you.
why: Wald wrote eight memoranda in 1943 on estimating aircraft vulnerability from returning planes; Mangel and Samaniego summarised them in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (1984).
The same reasoning applies wherever data has passed through a filter, from investment fund records to medical trials that lose drop-outs.
Caveat: the famous red-dotted plane picture is a later illustration, and some dramatic details of the popular story are embellished. The statistical point stands.

visual.note: The bomber story, then how the same filter distorts everyday judgements.

ideas.deep_dive:
Wald, born in 1902 in Cluj, was a Jewish mathematician who emigrated to the United States and joined Columbia's Statistical Research Group, a wartime team formed in 1942 that also included Milton Friedman and George Stigler. It answered statistical questions from the military, from bombing accuracy to quality testing.

His surviving work on aircraft is a set of eight memoranda written around 1943. They don't contain the famous dialogue or a recommendation to armour the engines; those details are later reconstruction. What they do contain is the hard part: a method for estimating how likely a plane was to be lost when hit in a given area, using only the planes that came back. If returning planes rarely show hits in one area while hits elsewhere are common, the likeliest explanation is that planes hit there didn't return.

The general rule: whenever your sample has passed through a filter, the filter shapes what you see. Successful companies, surviving funds, published studies, buildings still standing, patients who finished a trial: each is what's left after failures dropped out. Lessons drawn only from them can be exactly backwards.

The fix is to ask what the filter was and go looking for the missing cases. The limit: you can't always recover them, and sometimes survivors really are better. The point is to know which situation you're in.

examples.title: The bomber memoranda
examples.text: Wald's eight memoranda were declassified and published in 1980–81. They set out a "basic equation" for estimating a plane's chance of surviving hits in each area from returning-plane data. His colleague W. Allen Wallis later credited Wald with the survivor reasoning. The red-dotted plane picture everyone shares was drawn decades later, as an illustration.

examples.title: Fund league tables
examples.text: Investment performance tables usually show funds that still exist. S&P's SPIVA scorecard found that of US domestic equity funds in existence 20 years before the end of 2020, only about 32% were still going; the rest had been merged or closed. Average only the survivors and you quietly leave out much of the failure.

examples.title: Cats that fall from high-rises
examples.text: In 1987 vets at New York's Animal Medical Center reported on 132 cats that had fallen from buildings, and found those falling from higher floors had less severe injuries than those from lower down. One theory is that cats relax once they reach top speed. But cats killed by a fall are far less likely to be brought to a vet, so the data may simply be missing the worst cases.

images.caption: The famous illustration: hypothetical hits on planes that returned. The clean areas are where a hit was most likely fatal.
images.credit: Martin Grandjean, McGeddon, Cameron Moll / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ideas.title: Spread-out study beats cramming
ideas.idea:
You'll remember far more if you split the same study time into sessions spread over days, rather than cramming it into one sitting. Hermann Ebbinghaus first measured this in the 1880s by memorising nonsense syllables and testing himself: memories faded fast, but each well-timed review flattened the forgetting curve. More than a century later, a 2006 review led by Nicholas Cepeda pooled 839 comparisons from 317 experiments and confirmed that spaced practice reliably beats massed practice. It also found a handy rule: the longer you need to remember something, the bigger the gaps between reviews should be.

Cramming feels productive because the material is fresh in the moment. That fluency is misleading. The effort of recalling something half-forgotten is what makes it stick.
why: Ebbinghaus, Memory (1885), mapped the forgetting curve using himself as the only subject.
Cepeda and colleagues, Psychological Bulletin (2006): the ideal gap between sessions grows with how long you need to retain the material.
Caveat: most studies use verbal recall, like vocabulary. Spacing seems to help complex skills too, but that evidence is thinner.

ideas.deep_dive:
Ebbinghaus's method was gruelling. He memorised lists of three-letter nonsense syllables, so meaning couldn't help, then measured how much effort it took to relearn them after different delays. Memory dropped steeply in the first hours and days, then levelled off. Crucially, each relearning made the next decline slower.

Cepeda and colleagues' 2006 review found the spacing effect robust across hundreds of experiments, and showed that the best gap between sessions grows with how long you need to remember. For a test next week, review after a day or so; for something you need next year, gaps of weeks work better.

Why does it work? A leading explanation is that recall that takes effort strengthens memory more than easy rereading. When you return after a gap and have to dig the answer out, you rebuild a stronger, more retrievable memory. Cramming feels better because everything is fresh, but that fluency is borrowed and fades fast. It also fools you into thinking you know the material better than you do.

The practical form is spaced retrieval: test yourself rather than rereading, and review just as things start to slip. The limit: most evidence comes from facts and vocabulary. For complex skills and deep understanding, spacing still seems to help, but the evidence is thinner and other methods matter too.

examples.title: Leitner's box
examples.text: In 1972 the German science writer Sebastian Leitner published a simple paper system: flashcards in a row of boxes. Get a card right and it moves to the next box, reviewed less often; get it wrong and it goes back to box one. It schedules spaced review automatically, and it's still one of the easiest ways to do it by hand.

examples.title: Duolingo's forgetting model
examples.text: Duolingo launched in 2012 with a Leitner-style schedule, then built a model that predicts how quickly each learner forgets each word. In tests reported in 2016, its prediction error was nearly half that of the Leitner system, and learners using it were 12% more active day to day. Your phone app is spacing your reviews for you.

images.caption: The forgetting curve: memory falls fast after learning, and each well-timed review slows the next fall.
images.credit: Via Wikimedia Commons (author and licence on the file page)

ideas.title: Efficiency can raise consumption
ideas.idea:
Making something more efficient can increase how much of it we use, not reduce it. In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons spotted a puzzle in Britain's coal figures. James Watt's improved steam engine burned far less coal for the same work, yet national coal consumption kept soaring. Cheaper power made steam worth using in mines, mills and factories that couldn't justify it before, so total demand grew faster than efficiency saved. Jevons concluded that using fuel economically does not mean using less of it.

Economists now call this the rebound effect. Fuel-efficient cars tempt people to drive further; cheaper computing gets spent on ever bigger models. Efficiency is still worth having, but if the aim is to use less, it usually needs a cap or a price signal alongside it.
why: William Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question (1865).
Later economists, including Khazzoom, Brookes and Saunders, extended the idea from single products to whole economies.
Caveat: full 'backfire', where total use actually rises, is debated. In most single markets the rebound is partial, so efficiency still cuts use.

ideas.deep_dive:
Jevons published The Coal Question in 1865, and his worry was national: Britain's industrial power rested on cheap coal that would one day run short. Many assumed more efficient engines would stretch supplies. Jevons argued the reverse. Every gain in efficiency made steam power cheaper, which opened up uses that hadn't been worth it before, from pumping deeper mines to driving more mills, ships and railways. The new uses outgrew the savings.

Economists now call the general mechanism the rebound effect. When something gets more efficient, its effective price falls, so people use more of it, spend the savings on other things that also use energy, and whole industries grow around the cheaper input. If the rebound is less than the saving, efficiency still cuts use overall. If it's more, total use rises: the Jevons paradox, sometimes called backfire.

Backfire is most likely when demand is far from satisfied and the efficient thing is a general input, like energy, light or computing, that feeds many other activities. It's least likely for things we already have enough of: a more efficient fridge doesn't make you buy a second one.

The practical upshot: efficiency is valuable, but if the goal is to use less of a resource, pair it with something that locks in the savings, such as a cap, a price or a standard.

examples.title: Two centuries of light
examples.text: Roger Fouquet and Peter Pearson reconstructed the cost of lighting in the UK. Between 1800 and 2000, as candles gave way to gas and then electric bulbs, the price of a unit of light fell more than 3,000-fold. Total consumption of light rose about 40,000-fold. Each efficiency leap was spent on far more light, not on smaller bills.

examples.title: AI after DeepSeek
examples.text: In January 2025, when the Chinese lab DeepSeek showed a much cheaper way to build capable AI models and tech shares fell, Microsoft's Satya Nadella posted "Jevons paradox strikes again!", arguing that as AI gets more efficient and accessible, its use will skyrocket. Whether total AI computing and energy use rises as a result is being watched closely.
